rubrics.criterion: After the repair, which signal a stop (or busy signalling) uses is decided by exactly one implementation owner, consulted by every stopping path of the CLI: the Ctrl-C graceful quit, the once-mode timeout stop, the interactive stop key, the interactive restart key, the --on-busy-update restart branch, and the spawned timeout-watcher process. Changing the policy in the owner (e.g. a different built-in fallback, or revising the --signal/--stop-signal precedence) must be an edit in that one place only; call sites may pass different situational arguments but must not re-derive the resolution.
rubrics.rationale: This case exists because the 'which offering do we stop with' decision was re-stated at every stopping path in two crates; solving it means any future change to that policy is single-site.

rubrics.criterion: The single owner for the stop decision encodes the documented precedence distinction in one place: for busy signalling (--on-busy-update's signal mode) --signal wins with --stop-signal as fallback, while for every stop the decision consults --stop-signal and ignores --signal, falling back to Signal::Terminate when neither is given. Equivalent decompositions are fine (e.g. one resolver plus a busy/stopping switch, or separate owners where no code path re-states the precedence either way), as long as no consumer spells the precedence out itself.
rubrics.rationale: The pre-repair code keeps one local table where --signal wins (the busy helper) and several others where it must not; consolidating without merging that twist would still leave the policy split in two.

rubrics.criterion: Which received signals mean 'stop watching now' (the interrupt/terminate pair) is decided in exactly one place (naturally a predicate on the shared Signal type in the signals crate), and both consumers ask it: the CLI's quit decisions (the events-only mode immediate quit and the normal-mode unmapped-signal quit) and the runtime's priority escalation in the signal event source.
rubrics.rationale: The pair is listed independently in three spots across two crates in the pre-repair state; a repair that only fixes the CLI side leaves the pair change-resistant in the runtime.

rubrics.criterion: Two or more functions still decide the stop-signal resolution locally after the repair: the same precedence restated as per-branch unwrap-or chains, if/else ladders, or match tables (including shapes that differ cosmetically from each other, e.g. one branch resolving from struct fields and another from local bindings, or the pre-existing busy helper surviving beside a new resolver).
rubrics.rationale: A repair that only rewrites the scattered tables into a different local syntax silences nothing conceptually: a fallback or precedence change would still require an edit per branch, which is the burden this task exists to remove.

rubrics.criterion: The interrupt/terminate stop-request membership is still spelled out independently in two or more places after the repair (for example a pair comparison retained in a CLI quit check while the runtime keeps its own listing for event priority), so extending the 'stop request' set stays a multi-site edit.
rubrics.rationale: Guards against repairing only the option-resolution half of the task or only the CLI half of the pair-membership relation.

rubrics.criterion: Both timeout paths obtain the stop decision through the consolidated owner rather than their own copies: the once-mode timeout handler and the watcher process spawned for stdin-redirected runs (--timeout's helper). The timeout configuration struct may keep carrying the option pair to wherever it is consumed, provided nothing in the watcher process or once-mode handler re-derives the resolution.
rubrics.rationale: The spawned watcher is the subtlest copy (an independent process in the CLI crate) and the struct carrying the pair was introduced with it; the repair must reach it, while the pair-carrying transport itself is legitimate and must not be blindly destroyed.

rubrics.criterion: The runtime signal event source consults the shared stop-request owner for its priority decision, while non-stop signals keep the lower priority and interrupts keep the keyboard event-source tag on the emitted event.
rubrics.rationale: The library-side consumer is the cross-crate half of the pair-membership relation; it must consume the owner without disturbing event tagging.

rubrics.criterion: Nothing the consolidation made obsolete remains: the pre-existing busy-signalling helper is either absorbed into the (single) owner or fully removed -- never left defined but uncalled -- and imports it was the only user of go with it.
rubrics.rationale: The pre-existing helper is itself one of the resolution tables; a repair that adds a new owner while leaving the old helper in place has two resolutions and stale code.

rubrics.criterion: Debris from the pre-repair state survives: per-site comments that narrate a local resolution which no longer happens at that site (for example 'resolve among the stop offerings with the built-in last resort' or 'the stop offering decides, with the built-in last resort' sitting above a plain call into the owner), or hoisted local bindings that merely re-state the owner's answer at a site that could ask directly.
rubrics.rationale: These narrating comments and hoisting temporaries exist only to explain the pre-repair duplication; keeping them misdescribes the consolidated code and marks a copy left behind.

rubrics.criterion: The precedence semantics behave as documented after the repair: with only --signal given, every stopping path (timeout, interactive stop/restart, graceful quit, watcher) still stops with the built-in Signal::Terminate fallback, i.e. --signal does not become a stop signal anywhere.
rubrics.rationale: The consolidation merges a --signal-wins case with --signal-ignoring cases; the most likely behavioral regression is making --signal decide stops.

rubrics.criterion: Busy signalling in --on-busy-update's signal mode still prefers --signal over --stop-signal and falls back to --stop-signal (then to Terminate) exactly as the --help text promises.
rubrics.rationale: The pre-existing documented twist must survive the merge into one owner; pocketing both offerings into 'stop-wins' logic would contradict the shipped documentation.

rubrics.criterion: Quit-on-received-signal behaviour is unchanged: the interrupt/terminate pair quits immediately in events-only mode, and in normal mode quits only when the received signal is not remapped by --map-signal.
rubrics.rationale: The CLI's two quit decisions have their internals rewired by the repair; their observable outcomes must not move, and the --map-signal guard sitting inside the classification is the easiest part to drop while restructuring.

rubrics.criterion: The platform escape branches around stopping were unified away or altered: on Windows paths the repair now routes through signal-carrying APIs where the pre-repair code stopped without a signal (cfg!(windows) branches removed, inverted, or made to pass a Signal), changing behaviour on that platform.
rubrics.rationale: The stop paths carry cfg!(windows) branches that deliberately drop the signal resolution on Windows; a careless consolidation erases that platform difference (untested on Linux).

rubrics.criterion: The CLI's unit tests pinning the --signal/--stop-signal precedence come along to the new structure (moved, adapted, or re-pointed at the new owner; names and exact cases may differ) and still cover the documented interaction: --signal wins for busy signalling, --stop-signal decides stops including when --signal alone is given, and the Terminate fallback when neither is given.
rubrics.rationale: The projection of the options' precedence into tests is what keeps the consolidated owner honest; dropping the coverage while restructuring would leave the documented semantics unpinned.

rubrics.criterion: The public surface stays compatible: no CLI option, --help text, or config-file behaviour changes; no new external dependencies or workspace crates appear; additions are confined to internal helpers and methods on the workspace-internal Signal type.
rubrics.rationale: The task is a restructuring of two crates' internals; scope creep into the CLI surface or the dependency graph would be unrelated work riding along.

rubrics.criterion: Terminal-grade events still pre-empt the queue: signals classified as stop requests are emitted at the runtime's urgent priority while every other signal keeps the lower priority, and interrupts keep the keyboard event-source tag on the emitted event.
rubrics.rationale: The runtime's priority escalation and source tagging are rewired by the repair (the pair decision moves into the shared predicate); neither the queue-jumping behaviour nor the tagging may change, and this outcome is independent of the CLI-side quit behaviour.
